'''Lucyan David Mech''' ({{IPAc-en|m|iː|tʃ}};<ref>{{Cite web |last=Mech |first=L. David |title=Dave Mech |url=http://davemech.org/ |access-date=July 14, 2020 |quote=pronounced 'Meech'}}</ref> born January 18, 1937), also known as '''Dave Mech''', is an American [[biologist]] specializing in the study of [[Wolf|wolves]]. He is a senior research scientist for the [[U.S. Geological Survey]] and an adjunct professor at the [[University of Minnesota]]. He has researched wolves since 1958 in locations including northern [[Minnesota]], [[Isle Royale]],  [[Alaska]], [[Yellowstone National Park]], [[Ellesmere Island]], and Italy.

Mech is the founder of the [[International Wolf Center]] and the vice-chair of its board of directors. The project to create the facility, which he started in 1985, was an outgrowth of his wolf research as well as his ambition to educate people about the nature of wolves, so that they may come to respect the creature through understanding.

He has published eleven books about wolves and other wildlife, including ''The Wolf: The Ecology and Behavior of an Endangered Species'' (1970) and ''Wolves: Behavior, Ecology, and Conservation'', which he co-edited with Luigi Boitani (2003). His 1997 book ''The Arctic Wolf: Ten Years with the Pack'' received an honorable mention by the [[National Outdoor Book Award]] (Nature and the Environment category). His latest book, with Doug Smith and Dan MacNulty, is ''Wolves on the Hunt:  the Behavior of Wolves Hunting Wild Prey''.

==Early life and education==
[[File:Wolves of Isle Royale (1966) Wolves vs Moose.png|thumb|200px|1966 photo by David Mech: Wolves holding moose at bay at Isle Royale]]
Mech was born in [[Auburn, New York]], on January 18, 1937, and raised in [[Syracuse, New York|Syracuse]].<ref name = "Purdue2005"/> He obtained a [[Bachelor of Science|B.S.]] degree in conservation from [[Cornell University]] in 1958<ref name="Purdue2005">{{Cite web |date=2005 |title=2005 Honorary degree |url=https://news.uns.purdue.edu/html3month/2005/05Hondocs/05.MECH.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20050527072143/http://news.uns.purdue.edu/html3month/2005/05Hondocs/05.MECH.html |archive-date=May 27, 2005 |access-date=July 3, 2018 |publisher=[[Purdue University]]}}</ref> and a Ph.D. in wildlife ecology from [[Purdue University]] in 1962.<ref name = "Purdue2005"/><ref name="ChicagoTribune">''Keeping the Wolf from Death's Door – Saving a Species by learning its secrets'' by Peter Gorner, photos by Frank Hanes  Chicago Tribune Magazine, April 9, 1989 Pages: cover, 10–13, 15–17, 20 {{Better source needed|reason=Reference is not a clickable link, and thus, its reliability is uncertain.|date=January 2025}}</ref>

From 1958 to 1962, Mech was a graduate student at Purdue, studying the wolves of [[Isle Royale]], on Lake Superior,<ref name="TheFarReach">{{Cite journal |last=Breining |first=Greg |date=January–February 2004 |title=The Far Reach: The lifework of a Minnesota biologist circles the world |url=https://apps.dnr.state.mn.us/volunteer_index/api/v1/article_pdf?id=2102 |journal=Minnesota Department of Resources Conservation Volunteer Magazine |pages=32–41}}</ref><ref name="ChicagoTribune" /> beginning in 1958.<ref name ="DuluthNewsTribune"> https://www.duluthnewstribune.com/sports/northland-outdoors/how-the-isle-royale-wolf-moose-study-began ''How the Isle Royale wolf-moose study began'' The Duluth News Tribune, December 11, 2020 by John Myers retrieved 1/7/2025 </ref> His first book was ''The Wolves of Isle Royale'', published in 1966 by the [[United States Department of the Interior|Department of the Interior]], having evolved from his doctoral thesis.<ref name = "TheFarReach"/> In 1966, he studied wolves in the [[Superior National Forest]] in Minnesota.<ref name ="TheFarReach"/><ref name="ChicagoTribune" />

==Career and research==
[[File:L. David Mech studying Arctic wolves.png|thumb|David Mech studying Arctic wolves]]

Beginning in 1986, Mech spent 25 summers observing wolves on [[Ellesmere Island]].<ref name="NationalGeographic2019">{{Cite journal |last=Shea |first=Neil |date=September 2019 |title=Alone with wolves |journal=[[National Geographic]] |pages=117–133}}</ref> He said that his research on the wolves there was different, because it is one of the few places where they are not afraid of people, making that experience one of the best in his life.<ref name="DaveMechFilm">{{Cite AV media |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JPDnz48BDqM |title=Dave Mech |date=January 26, 2009 |publisher=Conservation Minnesota |via=YouTube}}</ref> In addition, there were no trees or bushes to hide wolves from view in the [[tundra]]. In the summer, Mech found a den near the military and weather base at [[Eureka, Nunavut|Eureka]]. He witnessed wolf interactions within a family unit and watched them hunting [[muskox]]en; this type of research had not been done before. In an interview, Mech said, "The kind of stuff I got here was not just the objective behavioral stuff, but the kind of thing you get from living with a pet of some sort. You get an insight into the thing. You get to know the animal."<ref name ="TheFarReach"/> Mech and photographer [[Jim Brandenburg (photographer)|Jim Brandenburg]] together produced several articles and a film for National Geographic.<ref name =TheFarReach/> The Ellesmere research concentrated on observing the interactions of pack members with each other and with pups around a den. The study also encompassed wolf interactions with muskoxen and [[arctic hare]]s and wolf movements throughout the year using GPS collars.<ref name="ChicagoTribune" /><ref name = "UofMDataPage"/>

Mech's research involves monitoring wolf–deer relations in the Superior National Forest of Minnesota, examining relations between the two populations as well as the effects of snow conditions and [[canine parvovirus]] on that system.<ref name="ChicagoTribune" /> He has also conducted research in [[Denali National Park]], Alaska; [[Ellesmere Island]], Nunavut, Canada; and in [[Yellowstone National Park]]. The Denali work involved studying the interactions between wolves and caribou, moose, and [[Dall sheep]]. The Yellowstone National Park studies concentrated primarily on wolf interactions with prey, including mortality and survival studies of elk.<ref name = "UofMDataPage">[https://fwcb.cfans.umn.edu/personnel/david-mech University of Minnesota information page on David Mech] Retrieved March 4, 2017</ref>

Mech serves as a senior research scientist for the [[United States Geological Survey]] (USGS) since 1999, and prior to that, he was a wildlife research biologist in the Biological Resources Division of the USGS, from 1969 to 1999.<ref name="USGeologicalSurvey">{{cite web|title=David Mech, PhD |url=https://www.usgs.gov/staff-profiles/david-mech |website=usgs.gov |access-date=January 8, 2025}}</ref>

===Positions===
An avid mushroom hunter and fur trapper, Mech has continued to support fishing, hunting, and trapping, which has led to criticism from animal protectionists.<ref name="ChicagoTribune" /> He believes that states can manage wolves sustainably and that states where wolves are no longer on the endangered list should determine how the animal should be managed.<ref name="WolfManagementByMech">{{Cite web |last=Mech |first=David |date=June 13, 2018 |title=Mech View of Wolf Management |url=https://davemech.com/ |website=davemech.com}}</ref><ref name="SelfCorrecting">{{Cite web |last=Nock |first=Ban |date=February 16, 2013 |title="Science is self correcting" – on Wolves |url=https://www.dailykos.com/stories/2013/2/16/1168581/--Science-is-self-correcting-on-Wolves |access-date=February 16, 2017 |website=Daily Kos}}</ref> On his website, he lists [[mink]] trapping as one of his  interests.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Personal Interests |url=https://davemech.com/personal-interests/ |website=davemech.com}}</ref> He closed the abstract to "Is science in danger of sanctifying the wolf?", published in the January 2012 issue of ''[[Biological Conservation (journal)|Biological Conservation]]'', with "The wolf is neither a saint nor a sinner except to those who want to make it so."<ref name="sanctifying">{{Cite journal |last=Mech |first=L. David |date=January 2012 |title=Is science in danger of sanctifying the wolf? |url=http://www.floridalupine.org/publications/PDF/Mech-2012-Is-Science-in-Danger-of-Sanctifying-the-Wolf.pdf |journal=Biological Conservation |accessdate=February 16, 2017 |archive-date=February 16, 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170216215948/http://www.floridalupine.org/publications/PDF/Mech-2012-Is-Science-in-Danger-of-Sanctifying-the-Wolf.pdf |url-status=dead }}</ref>

Mech was actively involved in the reintroduction of [[Wolf|gray wolves]] to areas from which they had disappeared through human activities. After more than 45 years of population recovery, in 2020, the [[United States Fish and Wildlife Service|US Fish and Wildlife Service]] removed the gray wolf from the list of endangered species.<ref>{{cite web|title=Trump Administration Returns Management and Protection of Gray Wolves to States and Tribes Following Successful Recovery Efforts |url=https://www.doi.gov/pressreleases/trump-administration-returns-management-and-protection-gray-wolves-states-and-tribes |website=doi.gov |date=October 29, 2020 |access-date=January 6, 2025}}</ref> The [[Mexican wolf|Mexican]]{{Citation needed|date=January 2025}} and [[Red wolf|Red wolves]] remain on the list, however.<ref>{{cite web|title=Red Wolf |url=https://endangeredlist.org/animal/red-wolf/ |website=endangeredlist.org |access-date=January 6, 2025}}</ref>

Mech has also written about wolf management through regulation. According to him, every year, a certain percentage of a wolf population must be [[Culling|killed]] by humans (in addition to natural mortality) to keep the population stable. According to his findings, about 50% of young wolves over 5–10 months old must be killed each year to bring a wolf population under control.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Fuller |first1=Todd K. |last2=Mech |first2=L. David |last3=Cochrane |first3=Jean Fitts|date=2003 |title=Wolf Population Dynamics |url=https://digitalcommons.unl.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1374&context=usgsnpwrc |journal=Wolves: Behavior, Ecology, and Conservation |publisher=DigitalCommons@University of Nebraska – Lincoln |access-date=January 6, 2025}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Mech |first1=L. David |date=2001 |title=Managing Minnesota's Recovered Wolves |url=https://digitalcommons.unl.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1404&context=usgsnpwrc&fbclid=IwAR2dFebN0VfyBWXTVjdM7AKYXuFN_fIFhGSEQf9GaNYwJIP2TWxYgmxajKs |journal=Carnivore Ecology and Management |page=70 |publisher=DigitalCommons@University of Nebraska – Lincoln |bibcode=2001usgs.rept..108M |access-date=January 6, 2025}}</ref> In a 2017 publication, he describes, among other things, livestock-depredation control in the United States.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Mech |first1=L. David |date=2017 |title=Where can wolves live and how can we live with them? |url=https://wolfwatcher.org/wp-content/uploads/2016/11/Where-can-wolves-live-and-how-can-we-live-with-them.pdf |journal=Biological Conservation |volume=210 |page=310 |publisher=Elsevier |doi=10.1016/j.biocon.2017.04.029 |bibcode=2017BCons.210..310M |access-date=January 8, 2025}}</ref>

Mech has declined to express an opinion on whether wolves should be hunted or trapped for their pelts, saying that his opinion on the subject is no better than that of anybody else.<ref name="ChicagoTribune" />

==Publications==
[[File:04 North Pole Wolf.jpg|thumb|David Mech with a wolf tranquilized in order to fit a GPS tracking device]]

Mech has published approximately 380 scientific papers and 100 popular articles about wolves and other wildlife. He has written eleven books.<ref name="ListOfMechBooksByMech">{{Cite web |title=Books |url=https://davemech.org/wolf-news-and-information/books/ |website=davemech.org}}</ref> These include  ''The Wolf: The Ecology and Behavior of an Endangered Species'' (1970), ''Wolves: Behavior, Ecology, and Conservation'', which he co-edited with [[Luigi Boitani]] (2003), and ''Wolves on the Hunt: The Behavior of Wolves Hunting Wild Prey'' (2015), with Doug Smith and Dan MacNulty. His 1997 book, ''The Arctic Wolf: Ten Years with the Pack'', received an honorable mention by the [[National Outdoor Book Award]] (Nature and the Environment category). The [[International Wolf Center]] lists approximately 140 articles written by Mech, published from 1987 to the present, primarily in scientific journals.<ref name="WolfCenterArticleList">{{Cite web |title=Articles by David Mech |date=August 2013 |url=http://www.wolf.org/wolf-info/basic-wolf-info/in-depth-resources/scientific-publications/ |access-date=February 15, 2017 |publisher=Wolf Center}}</ref>

==Awards==
In 2005, Purdue University conferred upon Mech an additional honorary degree, with the statement: "Mech's long-term studies of the wolf and other wild vertebrates have resulted in nearly 400 scientific, semi-technical and popular publications or articles. His scholarly contributions have expanded the understanding of wolf ecology more than any other individual. No one has written about, spoken of or debated the status and future of the wolf more than him. He has contributed to virtually every wolf conservation effort that the planet has seen in recent decades. In recognition of his accomplishments, Mech was awarded the Wildlife Society's highest honor in 1993, the [[Aldo Leopold]] Award. Purdue previously honored him as recipient of the Distinguished Agricultural Alumni Award in 1995 and the Distinguished Undergraduate Research Award in 2000".<ref name = "Purdue2005"/>
